model_note.S:
cc: Visible blood in urine without pain

HPI: 28 yo f. Patient reports: I first saw blood 5 days ago. The blood appears in the urine, not from the vagina. There is no flank or groin pain. The urine is pink-red without clots. It happened twice, throughout the stream. It stopped between episodes. I had a sore throat and a cold 2 days before the urine changed color; no strenuous exercise, trauma or procedure. It cleared on its own. There is no clear trigger. I have taken no treatment. This has never happened before. I saw pink-red urine twice.

Patient perspective: It stopped, so could we just wait?

PMH: Hypertension; no kidney stones or prior urinary disease.

PSH: Appendectomy at age 18; no urinary procedures.

Meds: Lisinopril 10 mg daily; no anticoagulants.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Former smoker, half a pack/day for 6 years; quit 2 years ago. One alcoholic drink weekly; no recreational drugs. Print-shop designer; cleans printing equipment with solvents twice weekly while wearing gloves, chemical names unknown. Lives with husband.

FH: My mother is sixty-two and she has high blood pressure.; My father died of a stroke when he was seventy-six.; I have one sister, she's thirty-two and she's healthy.; Kidney disease doesn't run in my family as far as I know.

ROS: Urinary - Reports hematuria. Denies dysuria. Denies frequency. General - Denies fever. Denies weight loss. Denies fatigue. Gastrointestinal - Denies nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.3 F oral, P 76 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Comfortable and well appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended; healed lower abdominal scar. Bowel sounds present. No focal abdominal or suprapubic tenderness. Tympanic over examined quadrants. Neither costovertebral angle is tender.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy, urine protein quantification and renal function; check blood pressure and pregnancy status; arrange prompt clinician review and nephrology referral if glomerular findings, proteinuria or impaired renal function are present; explain that the recent respiratory illness suggests a possibility but does not establish IgA nephropathy; review results within 1 week and seek urgent care for reduced urine, edema or heavy bleeding.

2. Use culture when urine findings or symptoms suggest infection; treat only supported infection and reassess hematuria after treatment; explain that apparent infection cannot automatically account for recurrent visible blood.

3. Arrange risk-based urology assessment if visible hematuria remains unexplained or recurs, with imaging/cystoscopy as the clinician indicates; explain that malignancy is less common at this age but persistent blood still needs investigation; give urgent precautions for clots, inability to void or dizziness. Clarify the solvent products and exposure duration; occupational history alone does not establish the cause.

model_note.S:
cc: Visible blood in urine without pain

HPI: 28 yo f. Patient reports: I first saw blood 2 weeks ago. The blood appears in the urine, not from the vagina. There is no flank or groin pain. The urine is pink-red without clots. It happened twice, throughout the stream. It stopped between episodes. I had a sore throat and a cold 2 days before the urine changed color; no strenuous exercise, trauma or procedure. It cleared on its own. There is no clear trigger. I have taken no treatment. This has never happened before. I saw pink-red urine twice.

Patient perspective: It stopped, so could we just wait?

PMH: Hypertension; no kidney stones or prior urinary disease.

PSH: Appendectomy at age 18; no urinary procedures.

Meds: Lisinopril 10 mg daily; no anticoagulants.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Former smoker, half a pack/day for 6 years; quit 2 years ago. One alcoholic drink weekly; no recreational drugs. Print-shop designer; cleans printing equipment with solvents twice weekly while wearing gloves, chemical names unknown. Lives with husband.

FH: My mother is sixty-two and she has high blood pressure.; My father died of a stroke when he was seventy-six.; I have one sister, she's thirty-two and she's healthy.; Kidney disease doesn't run in my family as far as I know.

ROS: Urinary - Reports hematuria. Denies dysuria. Denies frequency. General - Denies fever. Denies weight loss. Denies fatigue. Gastrointestinal - Denies nausea. Denies vomiting. Denies abdominal pain.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.3 F oral, P 76 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, R 16 rpm, Pulse Ox 99% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert. Comfortable and well appearing.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Abdomen not distended; healed lower abdominal scar. Bowel sounds present. No focal abdominal or suprapubic tenderness. Tympanic over examined quadrants. Neither costovertebral angle is tender.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy, urine protein quantification and renal function; check blood pressure and pregnancy status; arrange prompt clinician review and nephrology referral if glomerular findings, proteinuria or impaired renal function are present; explain that the recent respiratory illness suggests a possibility but does not establish IgA nephropathy; review results within 1 week and seek urgent care for reduced urine, edema or heavy bleeding.

2. Use culture when urine findings or symptoms suggest infection; treat only supported infection and reassess hematuria after treatment; explain that apparent infection cannot automatically account for recurrent visible blood.

3. Arrange risk-based urology assessment if visible hematuria remains unexplained or recurs, with imaging/cystoscopy as the clinician indicates; explain that malignancy is less common at this age but persistent blood still needs investigation; give urgent precautions for clots, inability to void or dizziness. Clarify the solvent products and exposure duration; occupational history alone does not establish the cause.
